client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away three months ago. Things I used to love doing, like cooking or going for walks, just feel completely pointless now. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: I'm so deeply sorry for the loss of your partner — the weight you're carrying right now makes complete sense, and it takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help. When we lose someone so central to our lives, the things we once loved can feel hollow because so much of their meaning was woven together with that person. I'm wondering, when you think about something like cooking or walking, what specific thoughts or memories come up for you in those moments?

client: When I think about cooking, I just picture us in the kitchen together — he always used to taste whatever I was making and give me this ridiculous over-the-top reaction like it was the best thing he'd ever eaten. Now when I stand there, it just feels like the silence is louder than anything else. I end up leaving without making anything, and then I feel guilty on top of everything, like I'm failing at even the basics.
therapist: That image of him tasting your cooking with those over-the-top reactions is so vivid and beautiful — it shows how much love and joy lived in those ordinary moments together, and of course the kitchen feels unbearable without him there. I also want to gently notice that you're being very hard on yourself by calling it "failing," when in reality leaving the kitchen is your mind and heart trying to protect you from an overwhelming wave of grief. I'm curious — if a dear friend told you they couldn't cook right now because it reminded them of someone they lost, what would you say to them?

client: I know what you're getting at, and honestly if a friend told me that, I'd tell them to be gentle with themselves and that it makes total sense. But it's so much harder to apply that to myself — it just feels different when it's me, like I should be handling this better somehow. I can't really explain why I hold myself to a different standard, but the guilt just kind of overrides everything else.
therapist: You just showed remarkable self-awareness there — you *know* the compassionate response, and you can see the double standard, even if you can't yet feel your way into applying it to yourself, and that gap is so common in grief. That guilt whispering "you should be handling this better" is worth gently questioning — where do you think that belief comes from, this idea that there's a way you *should* be grieving? I wonder if we can start to get curious about whose voice that actually is.

client: Honestly, I think part of it might be his family — they've been very stoic about the whole thing, very "keep moving forward" types, and I've been around them a lot these past few months. But I'm not totally sure that's all of it, because even before he passed I always felt like I needed to have things together, like falling apart wasn't really an option for me. Getting curious about it sounds fine in theory, but I'm worried that if I start pulling on that thread, it's just going to make me feel worse, not better.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — it's a very human instinct to avoid touching something painful when you're already carrying so much, and I want you to know we never have to pull on anything faster than feels safe for you. What you've noticed though is really significant: that this belief that "falling apart isn't an option" was already living in you before his family, before the loss, which suggests it's been quietly shaping how you treat yourself for a long time. I'm curious — can you recall an early moment in your life where you first learned that keeping it together was something you *had* to do?

client: There's this one memory that comes up — my mom went through a really hard time when I was about twelve, and I just kind of stepped up and became the steady one in the house because someone had to be. I don't think anyone explicitly told me to hold it together, it was more like I figured out that my falling apart would make everything worse for everyone else. I haven't thought about that in a long time, and I'm not sure how digging into something from that far back is going to help me get through tomorrow, you know?
therapist: What you just uncovered is really profound — at twelve years old, you taught yourself that your feelings were a burden to others, and that belief has been quietly running in the background ever since, including right now in your kitchen. Your concern about getting through *tomorrow* is completely valid too, and I don't want this to feel like we're wandering away from what you need right now. I'm wondering — knowing that this "stay steady" rule was something a twelve-year-old created to protect others, does it feel any different to consider that it might not be a rule you actually *have* to keep following today?

client: When you put it that way, I can kind of intellectually see that a twelve-year-old made that rule under pressure, and it wasn't exactly a free choice. But knowing that doesn't automatically make the feeling go away — it still feels really risky to let myself fall apart, like something bad will happen if I do, even though I can't say exactly what that something is. I guess I'm just not sure that understanding where it came from is enough to actually change anything.
therapist: You're touching on something really important — insight is often just the first small step, and you're right that understanding alone doesn't automatically rewire a feeling that's been protecting you for decades. That sense of "something bad will happen" is worth getting curious about, because it's likely that twelve-year-old's fear still speaking, warning you of a danger that made sense then but may not reflect your life now. I'm wondering — when you imagine actually allowing yourself to grieve fully, just for a moment, what is the worst thing you picture happening?

client: I think the worst thing I picture is just completely falling apart and not being able to put myself back together — like if I really let myself feel it, I'll just be useless, unable to function, and there'll be no one there to help me through it anyway. That's the part that scares me most, the "no one there" piece, because it's not like when I was twelve where at least my mom was in the house even if she was struggling. He was the person I would have leaned on for something like this, and that's just such a painful thing to sit with.
therapist: That last part is one of the most painful paradoxes of losing a partner — the very person you would have turned to for comfort in this grief is the one whose absence is causing it, and sitting with that is an enormous thing to carry alone. I also want to gently reflect back something courageous you just did: you let yourself feel the edges of that fear out loud, right here, and you didn't fall apart — you stayed present and articulate and real. I'm wondering, in this moment, does it feel even slightly different to notice that you're not completely alone in this, that you're here, reaching out, and being heard?

client: It does feel slightly different, yeah — there's something about saying it out loud and not having the world end that's a little surprising to me. But I also don't want to overstate it, because this is one hour and then I go home to that quiet apartment, and that's the part that feels impossible. I guess I'm just scared that whatever small thing I feel here won't survive contact with real life.
therapist: What you just described - saying something out loud and noticing the world didn't end - is actually exactly how change begins, not in one dramatic shift but in small moments of evidence that gently challenge the old rules. Your fear about the quiet apartment is real and valid, and I don't want to minimize it, but I'm curious whether we might think about one very small, low-pressure thing you could have waiting for you there tonight - not to fix the grief, but just to be a tiny bit less alone with it. What's one small thing, even something that feels almost too simple, that might make that return home even slightly more bearable?

client: I've been thinking about calling my sister, because she knew him too and she's been checking in on me, but I keep putting it off because I don't want to be a burden to her — which I realize even as I say it sounds like the same old pattern. Maybe I could just send her a text tonight, something small, not a whole emotional conversation, just enough to feel like someone knows I'm home. I'm still not totally convinced it'll help, but I suppose it's less scary than some of the other things we've talked about today.
therapist: You just caught yourself in that old pattern in real time — "I don't want to be a burden" — and then gently challenged it yourself, which is a genuinely meaningful moment. A simple text to your sister, someone who loved him too and who's already been reaching out to you, sounds like a beautifully small and honest first step, not a performance of vulnerability, just a quiet signal that you're there. I'm curious — what do you think it might feel like tomorrow, having sent it?

client: Honestly, I think it might feel like a small relief, like at least one person knows I made it through the day. But I also know myself well enough to know I might talk myself out of it by the time I get home, start thinking it's too late or that she's busy or whatever excuse comes up. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to make myself actually follow through, because the gap between deciding to do something in here and actually doing it out there feels pretty wide sometimes.
therapist: That gap between intention and action is so real, and your self-awareness about your own avoidance patterns is actually your greatest ally here — because you can see the excuse coming before it even arrives. One simple way to bridge that gap is to make the commitment more concrete right now, like deciding on a specific time tonight — say, within the first ten minutes of getting home — before your mind has a chance to negotiate. What would it look like to make that one small decision right now, while you're still in this space where it feels possible?
